meta.units: kcal; grams (g) for macros and fibre; mg for minerals and vitamin C. Carbs are available carbohydrate (fibre is listed separately), as in IFCT 2017.
meta.nutrition_method: For each ingredient with an amount: grams_used_for_nutrition x (per-100 g value of its food_id) / 100, summed over all ingredients, then divided by servings. grams_used_for_nutrition equals amount, except for grains and dals listed as cooked, which are converted to raw weight with cooked_to_raw_factor. Ingredients without an amount (salt to taste, water as needed) count as 0. nutrition_per_serving is rounded the way the tools show it (kcal whole, others 1 decimal); nutrition_per_serving_exact is unrounded.
notes: amount is for the whole recipe, not per serving.
food_id links to foods.json (type ingredient). Water and ice have no food_id (0 kcal, not in the food list).
name_hi is the Hindi dish name exactly as the tools display it (word-by-word dictionary translation).
jain_friendly is derived: vegan or vegetarian and no onion, garlic or root vegetables (the generator's "Jain" food group).
generator shows how the Diet Chart Generator uses the recipe: auto_planner false means it is offered only in Add food / Swap.

recipes.description: A thick, crisp, protein-rich Tamil dosa made from rice and four dals, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the rice, toor / arhar dal, chana dal, urad dal and moong dal well and soak together for 4–6 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Drain and grind with the ginger, green chilli and curry leaves and spices to a slightly coarse, thick batter, adding water as needed.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add salt and mix well. This batter needs no fermentation.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a medium-thick round. Sprinkle the topping over it and press lightly.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges and cook for 2–3 minutes until golden, then flip and cook for 1–2 minutes more.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Grind the batter slightly coarse for a crisp texture.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, avial or a little jaggery and butter (traditional).
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days.

recipes.description: A protein-rich gram flour pancake folded with creamy avocado and fresh vegetables, with healthy fats and plenty of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the besan and ripe avocado with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Dice the avocado and mix it with the lemon juice, roasted cumin, black pepper, chaat masala and hung curd. The lemon juice keeps it from browning.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Spread 2 tbsp of the filling over one half of the chila, fold it over and press lightly. Repeat with the remaining batter.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Use a ripe avocado that yields slightly to gentle pressure; avocado batter is softer, so do not spread it too thin.
Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A Tamil Nadu-style kambu (pearl millet) dosa, warming and rich in iron.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli and bajra and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A crisp, warming dosa made with pearl millet flour and semolina.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the bajra, rava / suji and rice flour and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the onion, green chilli, curry leaves and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Fluffy barnyard millet idlis, light and high in fibre.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the barnyard millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: Pretty pink instant idlis with beetroot purée.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the beetroot.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

recipes.description: A soft, orange-tinted dosa with carrot blended into the batter.

steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.text: Soak the idli for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.text: Finely chop the sweet corn kernels, capsicum, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Instant rava idlis with crushed sweet corn, soft and slightly sweet.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the sweet corn kernels.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the foxtail millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A Chennai street-style dosa filled with spiced chicken keema.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Sauté onion, ginger and garlic in oil, add tomato and masalas, then the chicken mince. Cook, breaking it up, for 10–12 minutes until fully cooked and dry.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A buckwheat flour chila for vrat days, earthy, filling and gluten-free.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the green chilli and coriander leaves and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the kuttu and potato with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 2 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion, tomato and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the foxtail millet in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the onion, green chilli, curry leaves and coriander leaves and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

recipes.description: A fibre-rich uttapam made with foxtail millet batter.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the foxtail millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, carrot, coriander leaves and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion, carrot, capsicum, cabbage and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A light, crisp dosa made from yellow moong dal, very easy to digest.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and rice well and soak together for 3–4 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Drain and grind with the ginger and green chilli and spices to a slightly coarse, thick batter, adding water as needed.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add salt and mix well. This batter needs no fermentation.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a medium-thick round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges and cook for 2–3 minutes until golden, then flip and cook for 1–2 minutes more.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Grind the batter slightly coarse for a crisp texture.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, avial or a little jaggery and butter (traditional).
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days.

recipes.description: Protein-rich idlis made with moong dal and rice, soft and light.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli and moong dal for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: Protein-rich instant idlis from ground moong dal, no rice needed.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Measure out the moong dal.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: A protein-rich instant uttapam made from moong dal batter.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: Mix the moong dal and rava / suji with curd, salt and water to a thick batter. Rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, tomato, coriander leaves and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Besan chila with moringa (drumstick) leaves, one of the most nutrient-dense greens.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the besan and moringa with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A dosa from rice and two millets, giving more fibre and minerals.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli, foxtail millet and little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal, chana dal and moong dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Delicate, soft, lace-thin Mangalorean rice dosas, traditionally served with coconut chutney or curry.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the rice flour with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the grated coconut. Rest for 10 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Fibre-rich instant appe with oats, crisp and light.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the rolled oats, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the onion, carrot, green chilli, coriander leaves and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

steps.text: Stir in the onion, green chilli, ginger, curry leaves and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A thick, soft South Indian pancake topped with caramelised onions and chillies.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, green chilli and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Besan chila loaded with fresh spinach for extra iron, folate and a lovely green colour.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the besan and spinach with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Green, iron-rich idlis with spinach purée in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Blend the blanched spinach to a smooth purée and gently fold it into the fermented batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: Moong dal chila blended with spinach, a bright green, iron-rich breakfast.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and spinach 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Crisp dosa filled with a spicy paneer bhurji, a protein-rich twist on masala dosa.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Sauté onion and capsicum in oil, add tomato, turmeric and pav bhaji masala and cook until soft. Add the crumbled paneer, salt and coriander and mix for 1 minute.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

steps.text: Add salt and mix well. This batter needs no fermentation.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a medium-thick round. Sprinkle the topping over it and press lightly.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges and cook for 2–3 minutes until golden, then flip and cook for 1–2 minutes more.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Grind the batter slightly coarse for a crisp texture.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, avial or a little jaggery and butter (traditional).
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days.

recipes.description: Instant ragi appe, soft, nutty and rich in calcium.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the ragi, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the onion, coriander leaves, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: A calcium-rich finger millet chila with an earthy flavour and a soft texture.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the ragi and besan with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp, calcium-rich finger millet dosa.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the ragi, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the onion, green chilli, curry leaves and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Soft, brown idlis made with ragi flour stirred into the batter, rich in calcium.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli and ragi for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: Instant ragi and semolina idlis, soft and rich in calcium.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the ragi and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: An instant calcium-rich ragi uttapam with vegetables.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: Mix the ragi and rava / suji with curd, salt and water to a thick batter. Rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, carrot, coriander leaves and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the red / matta rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Oats and besan chila with spinach, high in fibre and iron.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the rolled oats, besan and spinach with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Instant green idlis with oats and spinach, high in fibre and iron.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the rolled oats and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the spinach.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: Uttapam topped with fresh spinach and onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the spinach, onion and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A healthy dosa from mixed sprouts and rice, rich in vitamin C and protein.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the mixed sprouts and rice well and soak together for 2 hours (rice only).

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Drain and grind with the ginger, green chilli and curry leaves and spices to a slightly coarse, thick batter, adding water as needed.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add salt and mix well. This batter needs no fermentation.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a medium-thick round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges and cook for 2–3 minutes until golden, then flip and cook for 1–2 minutes more.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Grind the batter slightly coarse for a crisp texture.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, avial or a little jaggery and butter (traditional).
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days.

recipes.description: Soft, mildly sweet paniyaram with ragi, banana and jaggery, a wholesome snack.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the ragi and whole-wheat flour in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the jaggery, banana and grated coconut and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve warm as a snack.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: A vegan, protein-packed chila folded over spiced crumbled tofu.

steps.text: Finely chop the onion, tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Crumble the tofu, sauté it for 2 minutes with turmeric and capsicum, then add chaat masala and coriander.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Spread 2 tbsp of the filling over one half of the chila, fold it over and press lightly. Repeat with the remaining batter.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A soft, slightly spongy chila made with moong and urad dal for more protein.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and urad dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Crisp outside, soft inside South Indian dumplings made from idli batter and vegetables, using very little oil.

steps.text: Take the idli and urad dal in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings

steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the carrot, green peas and coriander leaves.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

recipes.description: A quick North-meets-South dosa made from whole-wheat flour, ready in 15 minutes.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the whole-wheat flour and rice flour with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the onion, green chilli, curry leaves and coriander leaves. Rest for 10 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Flaky layered paratha with carom seeds, light and good for digestion.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Lightly crush the ajwain between your palms to release its aroma.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the whole-wheat flour with the spices, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll & layer
steps.text: Roll a ball into a thin circle, brush with a few drops of oil, sprinkle flour, pleat it like a fan, coil into a spiral and roll again into a 6-inch paratha.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Karnataka’s rice flour flatbread with onion, dill and coconut.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the rice flour with the onion, suva, carrot, grated coconut and green chilli and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

recipes.description: The beloved Punjabi breakfast: whole-wheat flatbread stuffed with spiced mashed potato.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Mash the boiled potatoes until smooth, with no lumps. Mix in onion, green chilli, coriander, amchur, roasted cumin, chilli powder, garam masala and salt.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A warming winter thepla with bajra flour and fresh fenugreek.

steps.text: In a bowl, combine the bajra and whole-wheat flour with the methi, curd, sesame seeds, ginger and green chilli, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Roll

Best time: breakfast or lunch.

recipes.description: Bright pink parathas with beetroot and potato, rich in folate.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Squeeze the beetroot, mix with potato, chilli, coriander and the spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Naturally pink parathas with beetroot purée in the dough, a fun lunch-box bread.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Boil or steam the beetroot for 5 minutes and blend to a purée.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the whole-wheat flour with the beetroot, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: A light, nutty foxtail millet roti with a low glycaemic index.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the foxtail millet and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.
