recipes.description: A wholesome oats chila with cabbage, quick to make and full of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the rolled oats, besan and cabbage with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with carrot, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the carrot and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Instant dalia idlis with carrot.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the carrot.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer

recipes.description: A protein-rich green moong chila with carrot, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the whole green moong 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 6–8 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the carrot and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

steps.title: Add the flavourings

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with corn, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the sweet corn kernels and capsicum. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Instant dalia idlis with corn.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the sweet corn kernels.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: A wholesome jowar chila with corn, quick to make and full of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion, capsicum and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the jowar, besan and sweet corn kernels with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Serve

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the foxtail millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the carrot, green peas and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A foxtail millet dosa with potato masala.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the foxtail millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

recipes.description: Green foxtail millet idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the foxtail millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

recipes.description: A green kodo millet dosa with spinach purée.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the kodo millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the spinach and stir it into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Green kodo millet idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the kodo millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A wholesome bajra chila with lauki, quick to make and full of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the bajra, besan and lauki with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with lauki, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the lauki and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A thick little millet uttapam topped with carrot peas.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the carrot, green peas and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered

steps.title: Flip

Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A little millet dosa with a peppery mushroom filling.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Sauté garlic, onion and mushrooms on high heat until dry; season with pepper.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Green little millet idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the little millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with methi, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the methi and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Instant dalia idlis with methi.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the methi.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: Instant jowar idlis with methi.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the jowar and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the methi.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: A protein-rich masoor chila with methi, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 2 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the methi and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A wholesome multigrain chila with methi, quick to make and full of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the multigrain atta, besan and methi with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the rava / suji and curd with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A thick multigrain uttapam topped with carrot peas.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli, foxtail millet and little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the carrot, green peas and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A multigrain dosa with potato masala.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli, foxtail millet and little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds and urad dal, add curry leaves, ginger, green chillies and onion and sauté until soft. Add turmeric, the potatoes, salt and 3 tbsp water, mash lightly and mix in coriander.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Green multigrain idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli, foxtail millet and little millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with palak, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal and spinach 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Crisp moong dal appe with palak, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the moong dal in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the spinach, onion, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Spread 2 tbsp of the filling over one half of the chila, fold it over and press lightly. Repeat with the remaining batter.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Instant dalia idlis with peas.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia and rava / suji on low flame for 3–4 minutes until aromatic. Cool.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, chana dal, cashews, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger and fry until golden. Add this to the roasted base.

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Add curd, salt and enough water to make a thick, idli-like batter. Stir in the green peas.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Cover and rest for 15–20 minutes so the grains soften and swell.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil water in the steamer and grease the idli moulds.

steps.title: Add fruit salt
steps.text: Just before steaming, add the Eno with 1 tsp water and stir gently in one direction; the batter will turn frothy.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Fill the moulds immediately and steam for 10–12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Rest 2 minutes, demould and serve hot.

tips: Steam immediately after adding Eno; the bubbles fade if the batter waits.
Use fresh, slightly sour curd for the best taste.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: best eaten the same day; re-steam leftovers for 3 minutes.

recipes.description: Green ragi idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli and ragi for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A thick red rice uttapam topped with carrot peas.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the red / matta rice for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the carrot, green peas and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping

recipes.description: A red rice dosa with potato masala.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the red / matta rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds and urad dal, add curry leaves, ginger, green chillies and onion and sauté until soft. Add turmeric, the potatoes, salt and 3 tbsp water, mash lightly and mix in coriander.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Green red rice idlis with spinach.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the red / matta rice for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the spinach purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A wholesome bajra chila with spring onion, quick to make and full of fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the bajra, besan and spring onion with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with spring onion, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the spring onion and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the multigrain atta, besan and spring onion with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Aloo paratha made with bajra flour for extra fibre and minerals.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the bajra and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Mash the potatoes smoothly and mix in the onion and spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Soft bajra theplas with bathua.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop the bathua finely.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the bajra, whole-wheat flour and besan with the bathua leaves, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Bajra roti with carrot kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the bajra with the carrot and coriander leaves and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

steps.text: Squeeze the grated mooli very well and mix with the spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Bajra roti with lauki kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the bajra with the lauki and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the rolled oats and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Squeeze the grated mooli very well and mix with the spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Soft bajra theplas with palak.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop the palak finely.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the bajra, whole-wheat flour and besan with the spinach, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Makki roti with palak kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the makki with the spinach and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

recipes.description: Creamy barnyard millet porridge topped with apple cinnamon.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Lower the flame and cook for 18 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the dates. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Pour into bowls and top with the apple and walnuts.

recipes.description: Oats cooked the kanda poha way with broccoli.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion and broccoli and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice and coriander leaves and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

recipes.description: Dalia upma with corn capsicum.

steps.title: Roast the grain
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia on low flame for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until aromatic and lightly golden. Transfer to a plate.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai. Crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dals and cashews and fry until golden. Add curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion, sweet corn kernels and capsicum and sauté for 3–4 minutes until slightly soft.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: Add 480 ml water and salt and bring to a rolling boil.

steps.title: Add the grain
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the dalia in a thin stream with one hand while stirring continuously with the other, so no lumps form.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12–15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grain is soft.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the ghee, lemon juice and coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.

tips: Roasting the grain well keeps the upma fluffy and non-sticky.
For a softer upma, add ¼ cup more water.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, a cup of filter coffee or buttermilk.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Sprinkle a little water and reheat leftovers covered.

recipes.description: Oats cooked the kanda poha way with moong sprouts.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion and moong sprouts and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice and coriander leaves and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

recipes.description: Dalia upma with mushroom.

steps.title: Roast the grain
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia on low flame for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until aromatic and lightly golden. Transfer to a plate.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai. Crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dals and cashews and fry until golden. Add curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion and mushrooms and sauté for 3–4 minutes until slightly soft.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: Add 480 ml water and salt and bring to a rolling boil.

steps.title: Add the grain
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the dalia in a thin stream with one hand while stirring continuously with the other, so no lumps form.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12–15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grain is soft.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the ghee, lemon juice and coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.

tips: Roasting the grain well keeps the upma fluffy and non-sticky.
For a softer upma, add ¼ cup more water.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, a cup of filter coffee or buttermilk.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Sprinkle a little water and reheat leftovers covered.

steps.text: Add the onion, carrot, french beans, green peas and paneer and sauté for 3–4 minutes until slightly soft.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: Add 360 ml water and salt and bring to a rolling boil.

steps.title: Add the grain
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the quinoa in a thin stream with one hand while stirring continuously with the other, so no lumps form.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12–15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grain is soft.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the ghee, lemon juice and coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.

tips: Roasting the grain well keeps the upma fluffy and non-sticky.
For a softer upma, add ¼ cup more water.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, a cup of filter coffee or buttermilk.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Sprinkle a little water and reheat leftovers covered.

recipes.description: Creamy barnyard millet porridge topped with pomegranate.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the barnyard millet on low flame for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until aromatic.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Lower the flame and cook for 18 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the jaggery. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Pour into bowls and top with the pomegranate seeds and pistachios.

tips: Stir often and keep the flame low so the porridge does not catch at the bottom.
Porridge thickens as it cools; loosen it with a little warm milk or water.
serving_ideas: a handful of nuts or seeds and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in the fridge for 1 day. Reheat with a splash of milk or water.

recipes.description: Oats cooked the kanda poha way with pomegranate peanut.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice, coriander leaves and pomegranate seeds and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

recipes.description: South Indian sambar with avarakkai (flat beans).

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Wash the toor / arhar dal and pressure-cook with water and turmeric for 3–4 whistles until soft. Mash well.

steps.title: Soak the tamarind
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in ½ cup warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: In a pot, boil the sem, onion and tomato with 1¼ cups water and salt for 7–8 minutes until tender but not mushy.

steps.title: Add tamarind & spices
steps.text: Add the tamarind extract, sambar powder and jaggery and simmer for 5 minutes until the raw smell of tamarind goes.

steps.title: Add the dal
steps.text: Add the mashed dal, adjust the consistency with hot water and simmer for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard and methi seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing, and pour over the sambar.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Simmer the sambar after adding dal; boiling hard makes it lose its aroma.
Freshly ground sambar powder makes a big difference to flavour.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, idli, dosa or vada.
Best time: breakfast, lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: Chana dal cooked with bathua leaves, rich in iron and folate.

steps.title: Wash & soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 3–4 times until the water runs clear and soak for 60 minutes.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Cook the dal with the water, turmeric and salt for 3–4 whistles on medium flame, until completely soft. Let the pressure release naturally.

steps.title: Mash
steps.text: Open the cooker and whisk the dal lightly until creamy. Add hot water to get the consistency you like and simmer for 3–4 minutes.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the bathua leaves to the cooked dal and simmer for 4–5 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the tadka
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle the cumin and hing, add onion and sauté until golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli, then tomato, chilli powder and garam masala, and cook until the tomato turns soft and oil separates.

steps.title: Temper the dal
steps.text: Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal and cover immediately for 1 minute to trap the aroma.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Soaking dal makes it cook faster and easier to digest.
Add the tadka just before serving for the best aroma.
serving_ideas: phulka, jeera rice or brown rice, with a salad.
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: A light, peppery beetroot tomato rasam.

steps.title: Prepare the base
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in warm water for 10 minutes and extract the juice.

steps.title: Crush the spices
steps.text: Coarsely crush the pepper, cumin and garlic in a mortar.

steps.title: Boil the base
steps.text: In a pot, add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, turmeric, salt, jaggery, curry leaves, the crushed spices and rasam powder along with the beetroot. Boil for 7–8 minutes until the raw smell goes.

steps.title: Add water
steps.text: Add the remaining water. Heat until it turns frothy on top, then switch off. Do not boil it hard after this.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the rasam.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Add coriander, cover for 5 minutes, and serve hot with rice or as a soup.

tips: Switch off rasam as soon as it froths up; over-boiling makes it bitter.
Rasam tastes better after resting covered for 10 minutes.
serving_ideas: steamed rice with a little ghee, or sip it hot like a soup.
Best time: lunch or dinner; very soothing during colds.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: Curd-besan kadhi with bhindi lauki.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.text: Whisk the curd with the besan, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until completely smooth. Add the water and whisk again.

steps.title: Start cooking
steps.text: Pour into a heavy pot and bring to a boil on medium flame, stirring continuously so the curd does not split.

steps.title: Simmer
