recipes.description: Crisp jowar appe with beetroot, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the jowar, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the beetroot, onion, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: Crisp moong dal appe with beetroot, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the moong dal in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the beetroot, onion, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: A thick classic uttapam topped with beetroot onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the beetroot, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Pink classic idlis with beetroot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the beetroot purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A pink brown rice dosa with beetroot in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the brown rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the beetroot and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A brown rice dosa topped with grated carrot and coriander.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the brown rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle the carrot mixture over the dosa and press lightly.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend tomatoes with red chillies and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A thick classic uttapam topped with cabbage carrot.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the cabbage, carrot and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with cabbage, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and cabbage with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with capsicum, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the capsicum and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A protein-rich urad moong chila with capsicum, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and urad dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the capsicum and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Classic idlis with grated carrot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the carrot into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp jowar dosa with carrot.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the jowar, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the carrot, onion, green chilli and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A classic dosa topped with grated carrot and coriander.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle the carrot mixture over the dosa and press lightly.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the besan and chaulai with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the makki, besan and sweet corn kernels with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with dill, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the suva and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich urad moong chila with dill, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and urad dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the suva and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A pink foxtail millet dosa with beetroot in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the foxtail millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the beetroot and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Pink foxtail millet idlis with beetroot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the foxtail millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the beetroot purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A thick foxtail millet uttapam topped with beetroot onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the foxtail millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the beetroot, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Foxtail Millet idlis with fresh methi.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the foxtail millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the methi into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

steps.text: Soak the foxtail millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.text: Finely chop the mushrooms, onion and capsicum and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa

steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.

recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Kodo Millet idlis with crushed corn.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the kodo millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the corn into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the kodo millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the mushrooms, onion and capsicum and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with lauki, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and lauki with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the rajgira, besan and lauki with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A pink little millet dosa with beetroot in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the beetroot and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Pink little millet idlis with beetroot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the little millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the beetroot purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A thick little millet uttapam topped with beetroot onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the beetroot, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

steps.text: Wash the little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Prepare the filling
steps.text: Sauté onion and tomato, add soya and peas with spices and cook until dry.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A thick little millet uttapam topped with spinach onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the spinach, onion and green chilli and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with methi, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and methi with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Crisp jowar appe with methi, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the jowar, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the methi, onion, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp jowar dosa with methi.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the jowar, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the methi, onion, green chilli and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A wholesome rice flour chila with methi, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the rice flour, besan and methi with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with mooli, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the mooli and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich masoor chila with mooli, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 2 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the mooli and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A classic dosa with moringa leaves in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Stir the chopped moringa leaves into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the moringa and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A pink multigrain dosa with beetroot in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli, foxtail millet and little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the beetroot and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Pink multigrain idlis with beetroot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli, foxtail millet and little millet for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the beetroot purée into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A thick multigrain uttapam topped with beetroot onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli, foxtail millet and little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the beetroot, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fill & fold
steps.text: Place 2–3 tbsp of filling in the centre, fold the dosa over and lift onto a plate.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A thick multigrain uttapam topped with sprouts tomato.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the idli, foxtail millet and little millet for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the moong sprouts, tomato and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the idli, foxtail millet and little millet and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend tomatoes with red chillies and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with mushroom, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the mushrooms and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with mushroom, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and mushrooms with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Crisp jowar appe with mushroom, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the jowar, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the mushrooms, onion, green chilli and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich urad moong chila with mushroom, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the moong dal and urad dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 4 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the mushrooms and onion. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Crisp jowar appe with paneer, cooked with very little oil.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Take the jowar, rava / suji and curd in a bowl; it should be thick, like idli batter.

steps.title: Add the flavourings
steps.text: Mix in the paneer, onion, coriander leaves and fruit salt and salt.

steps.title: Heat the appe pan
steps.text: Heat a paniyaram (appe) pan on medium flame and add a few drops of oil to each cavity.

steps.title: Fill
steps.text: Pour batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3–4 minutes until the base turns golden.

steps.title: Turn
steps.text: Turn each appe with a skewer or spoon handle, add a drop of oil and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with coconut or tomato chutney.

tips: Keep the flame medium-low so the appe cooks through without burning.
Leftover idli or dosa batter is perfect for appe.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney or tomato chutney.
Great for tiffin boxes and evening snacks.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in a tiffin for 4–5 hours.
