steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: A protein-rich masoor chila with pumpkin, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 2 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the pumpkin and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: A pink red rice dosa with beetroot in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the red / matta rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend the beetroot and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: Pink red rice idlis with beetroot.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the red / matta rice for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment

recipes.description: A thick red rice uttapam topped with beetroot onion.

steps.title: Prepare the batter
steps.text: Soak the red / matta rice for 5 hours and the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours. Grind separately, mix, add salt and ferment overnight.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.text: Uttapam batter should be thicker than dosa batter; do not thin it.

steps.title: Chop the topping
steps.text: Finely chop the beetroot, onion and coriander leaves and mix them together.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Spread
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 5–6 inch round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle 2 tbsp of the topping evenly and press it in gently with the back of the ladle.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Drizzle oil around the edges, cover and cook on medium-low flame for 3 minutes until the base is golden.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip and cook the topping side for 1–2 minutes until lightly browned.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with chutney and sambar.

tips: Cooking covered on low heat makes the uttapam soft and fully cooked inside.
Press the topping into the batter so it does not fall off when flipped.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A red rice dosa topped with grated carrot and coriander.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the red / matta rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Sprinkle the carrot mixture over the dosa and press lightly.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: A tangy red rice dosa with tomato purée in the batter.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the red / matta rice and soak for 5–6 hours. Separately wash and soak the urad dal with the methi seeds for 4–5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water until light, fluffy and doubled in volume. Grind the soaked grain to a smooth paste. Mix both with clean hands.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and keep in a warm place for 8–12 hours (overnight) until the batter rises and smells mildly sour.

steps.title: Flavour the batter
steps.text: Blend tomatoes with red chillies and stir into the batter.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame. Sprinkle water; it should sizzle and evaporate. Wipe with an oiled cloth or half an onion.

steps.title: Spread the dosa
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in quick outward circles into a thin round.

steps.title: Crisp it up
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil or ghee over the dosa and cook on medium flame for 1–2 minutes until the base turns golden and crisp.

steps.title: Fold & serve
steps.text: Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve immediately.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Wipe the tawa with a damp cloth between dosas to cool it slightly so the batter spreads evenly.

tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter in a switched-off oven with the light on.
Use non-iodised salt for better fermentation.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: fermented batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days. Cooked dosas are best eaten fresh.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp jowar dosa with spinach.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the jowar, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the spinach, onion, green chilli and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with spring onion, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the tomato and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and spring onion with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: Classic idlis with crushed corn.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash and soak the idli for 5–6 hours. Separately soak the urad dal with methi seeds for 4 hours.

steps.title: Grind the dal
steps.text: Grind the urad dal with ice-cold water, a little at a time, to a light, fluffy, smooth batter.

steps.title: Grind the grain
steps.text: Grind the soaked grain to a slightly coarse, semolina-like batter. Mix both batters well with your hand.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Add salt, cover and leave in a warm place for 8–12 hours until it doubles and smells pleasantly sour.

steps.title: Add flavour
steps.text: Fold the corn into the batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.text: Boil 2 cups water in an idli steamer or pressure cooker (without the whistle). Grease the idli moulds lightly.

steps.title: Fill the moulds
steps.text: Gently stir the batter without knocking out the air and pour into the moulds until three-quarters full.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Steam on medium-high flame for 10–12 minutes. A toothpick inserted in the centre should come out clean.

steps.title: Rest & demould
steps.text: Rest for 2 minutes, then scoop out the idlis with a wet spoon and serve hot.

tips: Use a 4:1 ratio of idli rice to urad dal for soft idlis.
Do not over-stir fermented batter; it loses the air that makes idlis fluffy.
serving_ideas: sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
Best time: breakfast; also great for tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: batter keeps in the fridge for 3–4 days; steamed idlis keep for 1 day and can be re-steamed.

recipes.description: A wholesome dalia chila with sweet potato, quick to make and rich in fibre.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion and green chilli and grate the ginger. Small, even pieces keep the chila thin and help it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: In a mixing bowl, combine the dalia, besan and sweet potato with turmeric, ajwain, chilli powder and salt. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a smooth, lump-free batter that flows like dosa batter.

steps.title: Add vegetables & rest
steps.text: Fold in the chopped vegetables, ginger and coriander. Rest the batter for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the chila turns soft.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned iron tawa on medium flame and brush it with ¼ tsp oil. A few drops of water should sizzle when the pan is ready.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour one ladle of batter in the centre and spread it gently in circles into a 6–7 inch round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium-low flame for 2–3 minutes, until the top looks set and the edges lift easily and turn golden.

steps.title: Flip & cook
steps.text: Flip with a flat spatula and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney or curd. Make the remaining chilas the same way, adding only a few drops of oil each time.

tips: Rest the batter for 10 minutes; it makes the chila softer and easier to flip.
Keep the flame medium-low so the centre cooks before the outside browns.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Plain batter (without vegetables) keeps in the fridge in an airtight box for up to 12 hours.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp jowar dosa with tomato.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the jowar, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the tomato, onion, green chilli and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A protein-rich chana dal chila with tomato onion, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 5 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the onion, tomato and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: An instant, crisp ragi dosa with tomato.

steps.title: Mix the flours
steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the ragi, rice flour and rava / suji and curd with salt.

steps.title: Make a thin batter
steps.text: Add water gradually, whisking constantly, to make a thin, flowing batter without lumps — much thinner than regular dosa batter.

steps.title: Add flavourings & rest
steps.text: Stir in the tomato, onion, green chilli and coriander leaves. Rest for 20 minutes; the flour absorbs water, so thin it again before cooking.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat a cast-iron or non-stick tawa on medium-high flame and grease it lightly.

steps.title: Pour the dosa
steps.text: Stir the batter from the bottom and pour it from a height, starting at the edges and filling the gaps. Do not spread it with the ladle.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil and cook on medium flame for 3–4 minutes until the dosa turns golden and crisp and leaves the pan easily.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Fold and serve immediately; instant dosas lose their crispness as they cool. Stir the batter before each dosa.

tips: These dosas are cooked on one side only; flipping is not needed.
If the dosa sticks, the pan is not hot enough or needs a little more oil.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney and sambar.
Best time: breakfast or dinner.
recipes.storage: best made fresh. Leftover batter keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: A protein-rich masoor chila with zucchini, no fermentation needed.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 2–3 times and soak in plenty of water for 2 hours. Drain well.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind the soaked dal with ginger, green chillies and cumin, adding water little by little, to a smooth, thick batter. It should coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Add hing and salt and mix in the zucchini and coriander leaves. The batter does not need fermentation and can be used right away.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a non-stick or iron tawa on medium flame and grease it lightly with oil.

steps.title: Spread the chila
steps.text: Pour a ladle of batter and spread it quickly into a thin round. Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with green chutney or tomato chutney. Repeat with the remaining batter.

tips: Do not add too much water while grinding; a thick batter gives crisp chilas.
Soaking can be done overnight for a quicker morning.
serving_ideas: mint-coriander chutney, plain curd or raita, and a cucumber-tomato salad.
Best time: breakfast, or an early evening meal.
recipes.storage: Batter keeps in the fridge for up to 24 hours; stir and adjust with a little water before use.

recipes.description: Beetroot paratha made with bajra dough, a filling breakfast.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the bajra and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Squeeze the beetroot and mix with potato and spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Cabbage paratha made with bajra dough, a filling breakfast.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the bajra and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Salt the cabbage, rest 10 minutes, squeeze dry and add the spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.

Best time: breakfast or lunch.

recipes.description: Soft jowar theplas with bathua.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop or grate the bathua.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the jowar and whole-wheat flour with the bathua leaves, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Barnyard roti with carrot kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the barnyard millet with the carrot and coriander leaves and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side

recipes.description: Soft jowar theplas with carrot coriander, great for travel.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop or grate the carrot coriander.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the jowar and whole-wheat flour with the carrot, coriander leaves, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Beetroot paratha made with jowar dough, a filling breakfast.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the jowar and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Squeeze the beetroot and mix with potato and spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side

recipes.description: Soft bajra theplas with lauki.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop or grate the lauki.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the bajra, whole-wheat flour and besan with the lauki, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

recipes.description: Barnyard roti with methi kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the barnyard millet with the methi and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the jowar with the moringa and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

recipes.description: Beetroot paratha made with multigrain dough, a filling breakfast.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the multigrain atta with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Squeeze the beetroot and mix with potato and spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Rajma paratha made with multigrain dough, a filling breakfast.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the multigrain atta with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Mash the drained rajma and dry it in a pan; add spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve

steps.text: Mix the rolled oats and whole-wheat flour with salt and oil. Add water little by little and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the stuffing
steps.text: Mash the sweet potato and mix in the spices.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough and the stuffing into 4 equal portions each. The stuffing should be dry; moisture makes parathas tear.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Barnyard roti with onion kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the barnyard millet with the onion, coriander leaves and green chilli and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

recipes.description: Soft jowar theplas with palak.

steps.title: Prepare the add-ins
steps.text: Chop or grate the palak.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: In a bowl, combine the jowar and whole-wheat flour with the spinach, curd and sesame seeds, spices and salt. Add water gradually and knead into a soft dough. Rest for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the dough into 6 equal balls.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust a ball with flour and roll it into a thin 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Flip when small bubbles appear and cook the other side for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Apply a few drops of oil, flip and press gently with a spatula. Cook until both sides have golden-brown spots.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Keep warm in a cloth-lined box and serve with curd, chutney or a sabzi.

tips: Rest the dough so it rolls thin without shrinking back.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in an airtight box for 1 day at room temperature (theplas up to 3 days) and is ideal for travel.

steps.text: Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, place a portion of stuffing in the centre, gather the edges, pinch to seal and flatten gently.

steps.title: Roll
steps.text: Dust with flour and roll gently into a 6–7 inch paratha, applying even pressure so the stuffing does not break through.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa over medium flame. Cook for 1 minute until small bubbles appear, then flip.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Brush the cooked side with ½ tsp ghee or oil, flip again and press the edges with a spatula. Cook both sides until golden-brown spots appear.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with curd. Make the remaining parathas the same way.

tips: Seal the stuffing well and roll with light pressure to avoid tearing.
Use only ½ tsp ghee per side; dry-roasting first keeps the paratha light.
serving_ideas: plain curd or raita, a little white butter (optional) and pickle or green chutney.
Best time: breakfast or lunch.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot. Cooked parathas keep in a tiffin for 5–6 hours; the stuffing keeps in the fridge for 1 day.

recipes.description: Bajra roti with spring onion kneaded into the dough.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Take the bajra with the spring onion and salt in a wide plate.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.text: Add hot water little by little and mix with a spoon, then knead with the heel of your palm for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, crack-free dough. Millet dough has no gluten, so knead only one portion at a time.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Take a lemon-sized ball and pat it between your palms, or roll it between two sheets of butter paper, into a 6-inch round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place on a hot tawa on medium flame. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers to prevent cracks.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: When the bottom has light spots (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.

steps.title: Puff
steps.text: Roast directly on the flame with tongs, or press with a cloth on the tawa, until it puffs and both sides are cooked.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Apply a little ghee and serve hot.

tips: Knead each portion just before rolling; millet dough dries out quickly.
Patting with wet hands is easier than rolling for beginners.
serving_ideas: dal, sabzi, pithla or a garlic chutney, plus a little white butter or jaggery (traditional).
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten hot; it hardens as it cools.

recipes.description: Creamy dalia porridge topped with apple cinnamon.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia on low flame for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until aromatic.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Lower the flame and cook for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the dates. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Pour into bowls and top with the apple and walnuts.

tips: Stir often and keep the flame low so the porridge does not catch at the bottom.
Porridge thickens as it cools; loosen it with a little warm milk or water.
serving_ideas: a handful of nuts or seeds and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in the fridge for 1 day. Reheat with a splash of milk or water.

recipes.description: Barnyard Millet upma with beetroot.

steps.title: Rinse
steps.text: Rinse the barnyard millet and drain well.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai. Crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dals and cashews and fry until golden. Add curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion and beetroot and sauté for 3–4 minutes until slightly soft.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: Add 400 ml water and salt and bring to a rolling boil.

steps.title: Add the grain
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the barnyard millet in a thin stream with one hand while stirring continuously with the other, so no lumps form.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12–15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grain is soft.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the ghee, lemon juice and coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.

tips: Roasting the grain well keeps the upma fluffy and non-sticky.
For a softer upma, add ¼ cup more water.
serving_ideas: coconut chutney, a cup of filter coffee or buttermilk.
Best time: breakfast or a light dinner.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh. Sprinkle a little water and reheat leftovers covered.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai. Crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dals and cashews and fry until golden. Add curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and hing.

steps.text: Add the onion, carrot and french beans and sauté for 3–4 minutes until slightly soft.

steps.text: Add 420 ml water and salt and bring to a rolling boil.

steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the flavouring. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

recipes.description: Oats Poha cooked the kanda poha way with methi peas.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion, methi and green peas and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice and coriander leaves and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

recipes.description: Creamy dalia porridge topped with papaya.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia on low flame for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until aromatic.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Lower the flame and cook for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the dates. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Pour into bowls and top with the papaya and pumpkin seeds.

tips: Stir often and keep the flame low so the porridge does not catch at the bottom.
Porridge thickens as it cools; loosen it with a little warm milk or water.
serving_ideas: a handful of nuts or seeds and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in the fridge for 1 day. Reheat with a splash of milk or water.

recipes.description: Oats Poha cooked the kanda poha way with spinach corn.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion, spinach and sweet corn kernels and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice and coriander leaves and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

recipes.description: Creamy dalia porridge topped with strawberry.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: Dry-roast the dalia on low flame for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until aromatic.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Add the remaining toned milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring continuously so it does not stick.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Lower the flame and cook for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.text: Switch off the flame and stir in the honey. Adding jaggery off the heat stops milk from curdling.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Pour into bowls and top with the strawberries and almonds.

tips: Stir often and keep the flame low so the porridge does not catch at the bottom.
Porridge thickens as it cools; loosen it with a little warm milk or water.
serving_ideas: a handful of nuts or seeds and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; keeps in the fridge for 1 day. Reheat with a splash of milk or water.

recipes.name_hi: मीठा मक्का शिमला मिर्च ओट्स पोहा
recipes.description: Oats Poha cooked the kanda poha way with sweet corn capsicum.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Put the rolled oats and poha in a sieve and rinse under running water for 15–20 seconds, tossing gently. Drain and rest for 5 minutes to soften. Do not soak.

steps.title: Season the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle the turmeric, salt and sugar over the poha and fluff gently with a fork so they coat evenly.

steps.title: Roast the crunch
steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and roast the peanuts on low flame until crunchy. Remove and keep aside.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the mustard seeds and cumin, then add curry leaves, green chilli and hing.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: Add the onion, sweet corn kernels and capsicum and sauté on medium flame until the onion is soft and translucent and the vegetables are just tender (3–5 minutes).

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Add the seasoned poha and mix gently. Cover and cook on low flame for 2–3 minutes so it steams through.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Switch off the flame and add the lemon juice and coriander leaves and the roasted crunch. Toss gently and serve hot.

tips: Use thick poha; thin poha turns mushy.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the flame, or it turns bitter.
serving_ideas: a cup of masala tea or buttermilk, and a fruit.
Best time: breakfast or evening snack.
recipes.storage: best eaten fresh; it dries out when reheated.

steps.text: Lower the flame and add the rava / suji in a thin stream with one hand while stirring continuously with the other, so no lumps form.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 3–4 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grain is soft.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the ghee, lemon juice and coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.

tips: Roasting the grain well keeps the upma fluffy and non-sticky.

recipes.description: Chana dal cooked with baingan.

steps.title: Wash & soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 3–4 times until the water runs clear and soak for 60 minutes.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Cook the dal with the water, turmeric and salt and the brinjal for 3–4 whistles on medium flame, until completely soft. Let the pressure release naturally.

steps.title: Mash
steps.text: Open the cooker and whisk the dal lightly until creamy. Add hot water to get the consistency you like and simmer for 3–4 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the tadka
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle the cumin and hing, add onion and sauté until golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli, then tomato, chilli powder and garam masala, and cook until the tomato turns soft and oil separates.

steps.title: Temper the dal
steps.text: Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal and cover immediately for 1 minute to trap the aroma.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Soaking dal makes it cook faster and easier to digest.
Add the tadka just before serving for the best aroma.
serving_ideas: phulka, jeera rice or brown rice, with a salad.
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: South Indian sambar with capsicum onion.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Wash the toor / arhar dal and pressure-cook with water and turmeric for 3–4 whistles until soft. Mash well.

steps.title: Soak the tamarind
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in ½ cup warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: In a pot, boil the capsicum, onion and tomato with 1¼ cups water and salt for 7–8 minutes until tender but not mushy.

steps.title: Add tamarind & spices
steps.text: Add the tamarind extract, sambar powder and jaggery and simmer for 5 minutes until the raw smell of tamarind goes.

steps.title: Add the dal
steps.text: Add the mashed dal, adjust the consistency with hot water and simmer for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard and methi seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing, and pour over the sambar.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Simmer the sambar after adding dal; boiling hard makes it lose its aroma.
Freshly ground sambar powder makes a big difference to flavour.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, idli, dosa or vada.
Best time: breakfast, lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: A light, peppery carrot rasam.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Pressure-cook the toor / arhar dal with 2 cups water for 3 whistles and mash; keep the dal water.

steps.title: Crush the spices
steps.text: Coarsely crush the pepper, cumin and garlic in a mortar.

steps.title: Boil the base
steps.text: In a pot, add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, turmeric, salt, jaggery, curry leaves, the crushed spices and rasam powder along with the carrot. Boil for 7–8 minutes until the raw smell goes.

steps.title: Add water & dal
steps.text: Add the remaining water and the dal. Heat until it turns frothy on top, then switch off. Do not boil it hard after this.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the rasam.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Add coriander, cover for 5 minutes, and serve hot with rice or as a soup.

tips: Switch off rasam as soon as it froths up; over-boiling makes it bitter.
Rasam tastes better after resting covered for 10 minutes.
serving_ideas: steamed rice with a little ghee, or sip it hot like a soup.
Best time: lunch or dinner; very soothing during colds.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: A light, peppery coriander lemon moong rasam.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Pressure-cook the moong dal with 2 cups water for 3 whistles and mash; keep the dal water.

steps.title: Crush the spices
steps.text: Coarsely crush the pepper, cumin and garlic in a mortar.

steps.title: Boil the base
steps.text: In a pot, add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, turmeric, salt, jaggery, curry leaves, the crushed spices and rasam powder along with the coriander leaves. Boil for 7–8 minutes until the raw smell goes.

steps.title: Add water & dal
steps.text: Add the remaining water and the dal. Heat until it turns frothy on top, then switch off. Do not boil it hard after this.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the rasam.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Add coriander, cover for 5 minutes, and serve hot with rice or as a soup.

tips: Switch off rasam as soon as it froths up; over-boiling makes it bitter.
Rasam tastes better after resting covered for 10 minutes.
serving_ideas: steamed rice with a little ghee, or sip it hot like a soup.
Best time: lunch or dinner; very soothing during colds.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: Curd-besan kadhi with cucumber.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.text: Whisk the curd with the besan, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until completely smooth. Add the water and whisk again.

steps.title: Start cooking
steps.text: Pour into a heavy pot and bring to a boil on medium flame, stirring continuously so the curd does not split.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Once it boils, lower the flame and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens slightly and the raw besan smell goes.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the cucumber and simmer until tender.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil or ghee, crackle cumin, methi and mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the kadhi.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Use slightly sour curd for the best flavour.
Keep stirring until the kadhi comes to a boil to stop it from curdling.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice or khichdi.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

steps.text: Wash the masoor dal 3–4 times until the water runs clear and soak for 30 minutes.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Cook the dal with the water, turmeric and salt and the cauliflower for 3–4 whistles on medium flame, until completely soft. Let the pressure release naturally.

steps.title: Mash
steps.text: Open the cooker and whisk the dal lightly until creamy. Add hot water to get the consistency you like and simmer for 3–4 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare the tadka
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle cumin, add plenty of sliced garlic and fry until golden and crisp; switch off and add chilli powder and hing.

steps.title: Temper the dal
steps.text: Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal and cover immediately for 1 minute to trap the aroma.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Soaking dal makes it cook faster and easier to digest.
Add the tadka just before serving for the best aroma.
serving_ideas: phulka, jeera rice or brown rice, with a salad.
Best time: lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: South Indian sambar with lauki drumstick.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Wash the toor / arhar dal and pressure-cook with water and turmeric for 3–4 whistles until soft. Mash well.

steps.title: Soak the tamarind
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in ½ cup warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: In a pot, boil the lauki, drumsticks, onion and tomato with 1¼ cups water and salt for 7–8 minutes until tender but not mushy.

steps.title: Add tamarind & spices
steps.text: Add the tamarind extract, sambar powder and jaggery and simmer for 5 minutes until the raw smell of tamarind goes.

steps.title: Add the dal
steps.text: Add the mashed dal, adjust the consistency with hot water and simmer for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard and methi seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing, and pour over the sambar.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Simmer the sambar after adding dal; boiling hard makes it lose its aroma.
Freshly ground sambar powder makes a big difference to flavour.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, idli, dosa or vada.
Best time: breakfast, lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: Curd-besan kadhi with mixed greens.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.text: Whisk the curd with the besan, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until completely smooth. Add the water and whisk again.

steps.title: Start cooking
steps.text: Pour into a heavy pot and bring to a boil on medium flame, stirring continuously so the curd does not split.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Once it boils, lower the flame and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens slightly and the raw besan smell goes.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the spinach, methi and bathua leaves and simmer until tender.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil or ghee, crackle cumin, methi and mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the kadhi.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Use slightly sour curd for the best flavour.
Keep stirring until the kadhi comes to a boil to stop it from curdling.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice or khichdi.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: A light, peppery pepper cumin rasam.

steps.title: Prepare the base
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in warm water for 10 minutes and extract the juice.

steps.title: Crush the spices
steps.text: Coarsely crush the pepper, cumin and garlic in a mortar.

steps.title: Boil the base
steps.text: In a pot, add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, turmeric, salt, jaggery, curry leaves, the crushed spices and rasam powder along with the black peppercorns and cumin seeds. Boil for 7–8 minutes until the raw smell goes.

steps.title: Add water
steps.text: Add the remaining water. Heat until it turns frothy on top, then switch off. Do not boil it hard after this.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the rasam.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Add coriander, cover for 5 minutes, and serve hot with rice or as a soup.

tips: Switch off rasam as soon as it froths up; over-boiling makes it bitter.
Rasam tastes better after resting covered for 10 minutes.
serving_ideas: steamed rice with a little ghee, or sip it hot like a soup.
Best time: lunch or dinner; very soothing during colds.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: Curd-besan kadhi with pumpkin bhindi.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.text: Whisk the curd with the besan, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until completely smooth. Add the water and whisk again.

steps.title: Start cooking
steps.text: Pour into a heavy pot and bring to a boil on medium flame, stirring continuously so the curd does not split.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Once it boils, lower the flame and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens slightly and the raw besan smell goes.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the pumpkin and bhindi and simmer until tender.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil or ghee, crackle cumin, methi and mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the kadhi.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Use slightly sour curd for the best flavour.
Keep stirring until the kadhi comes to a boil to stop it from curdling.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice or khichdi.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: Curd-besan kadhi with raw banana.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.text: Whisk the curd with the besan, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until completely smooth. Add the water and whisk again.

steps.title: Start cooking
steps.text: Pour into a heavy pot and bring to a boil on medium flame, stirring continuously so the curd does not split.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Once it boils, lower the flame and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens slightly and the raw besan smell goes.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the raw banana and simmer until tender.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil or ghee, crackle cumin, methi and mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the kadhi.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Use slightly sour curd for the best flavour.
Keep stirring until the kadhi comes to a boil to stop it from curdling.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice or khichdi.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: A light, peppery spinach pepper rasam.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Pressure-cook the toor / arhar dal with 2 cups water for 3 whistles and mash; keep the dal water.

steps.title: Crush the spices
steps.text: Coarsely crush the pepper, cumin and garlic in a mortar.

steps.title: Boil the base
steps.text: In a pot, add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, turmeric, salt, jaggery, curry leaves, the crushed spices and rasam powder along with the spinach and black peppercorns. Boil for 7–8 minutes until the raw smell goes.

steps.title: Add water & dal
steps.text: Add the remaining water and the dal. Heat until it turns frothy on top, then switch off. Do not boil it hard after this.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat ghee, crackle mustard seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing and pour over the rasam.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Add coriander, cover for 5 minutes, and serve hot with rice or as a soup.

tips: Switch off rasam as soon as it froths up; over-boiling makes it bitter.
Rasam tastes better after resting covered for 10 minutes.
serving_ideas: steamed rice with a little ghee, or sip it hot like a soup.
Best time: lunch or dinner; very soothing during colds.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.description: South Indian sambar with sweet potato onion.

steps.title: Cook the dal
steps.text: Wash the toor / arhar dal and pressure-cook with water and turmeric for 3–4 whistles until soft. Mash well.

steps.title: Soak the tamarind
steps.text: Soak the tamarind in ½ cup warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.text: In a pot, boil the sweet potato, shallots and tomato with 1¼ cups water and salt for 7–8 minutes until tender but not mushy.

steps.title: Add tamarind & spices
steps.text: Add the tamarind extract, sambar powder and jaggery and simmer for 5 minutes until the raw smell of tamarind goes.

steps.title: Add the dal
steps.text: Add the mashed dal, adjust the consistency with hot water and simmer for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard and methi seeds, add dry red chillies, curry leaves and hing, and pour over the sambar.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Garnish with coriander and serve hot.

tips: Simmer the sambar after adding dal; boiling hard makes it lose its aroma.
Freshly ground sambar powder makes a big difference to flavour.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, idli, dosa or vada.
Best time: breakfast, lunch or dinner.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Dal thickens when cold; add hot water while reheating.

recipes.description: Chana dal cooked with zucchini.

steps.title: Wash & soak
steps.text: Wash the chana dal 3–4 times until the water runs clear and soak for 60 minutes.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Cook the dal with the water, turmeric and salt and the zucchini for 3–4 whistles on medium flame, until completely soft. Let the pressure release naturally.

steps.title: Mash
steps.text: Open the cooker and whisk the dal lightly until creamy. Add hot water to get the consistency you like and simmer for 3–4 minutes.

steps.text: Heat oil, crackle the cumin and hing, add onion and sauté until golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli, then tomato, chilli powder and garam masala, and cook until the tomato turns soft and oil separates.

steps.title: Temper the dal
steps.text: Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal and cover immediately for 1 minute to trap the aroma.

recipes.description: Chole cooked with corn in a homestyle masala.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Wash the kabuli chana well and soak in plenty of water for 8 hours or overnight.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Drain, add fresh water and salt and pressure-cook for 5–6 whistles until soft enough to mash between your fingers. Keep the cooking water.

steps.title: Make the masala
steps.text: Heat oil, add cumin and bay leaf. Add onion and sauté on medium flame for 8–10 minutes until deep golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli and cook 1 minute. Add the tomato purée and powdered spices and cook until the masala thickens and oil separates (6–8 minutes).

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the corn and cook 4 minutes.

steps.title: Combine
steps.text: Add the cooked kabuli chana with enough cooking water to make a gravy. Mash a few pieces against the side of the pan to thicken it.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Cover and simmer on low flame for 15 minutes so the kabuli chana absorb the masala.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the coriander leaves and lemon juice, check the salt and serve hot.

tips: Brown the onions slowly; this gives the gravy its depth without cream.
Use the legume cooking water in the gravy; it holds flavour and nutrients.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice, phulka or bhakri, with onion-cucumber salad.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2–3 days and tastes even better the next day. Freezes well for a month.

steps.text: Drain, add fresh water and salt and pressure-cook for 4 whistles until soft enough to mash between your fingers. Keep the cooking water.

steps.title: Make the masala
steps.text: Heat oil, add cumin and bay leaf. Add onion and sauté on medium flame for 8–10 minutes until deep golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli and cook 1 minute. Add the tomato purée and powdered spices and cook until the masala thickens and oil separates (6–8 minutes).

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the sweet potato and cook covered 8 minutes.

steps.title: Combine
steps.text: Add the cooked double beans with enough cooking water to make a gravy. Mash a few pieces against the side of the pan to thicken it.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Cover and simmer on low flame for 15 minutes so the double beans absorb the masala.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Add the coriander leaves and lemon juice, check the salt and serve hot.

tips: Brown the onions slowly; this gives the gravy its depth without cream.
Use the legume cooking water in the gravy; it holds flavour and nutrients.
serving_ideas: steamed rice, jeera rice, phulka or bhakri, with onion-cucumber salad.
Best time: lunch.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 2–3 days and tastes even better the next day. Freezes well for a month.

steps.text: Heat oil, add cumin and bay leaf. Add onion and sauté on medium flame for 8–10 minutes until deep golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli and cook 1 minute. Add the tomato purée and powdered spices and cook until the masala thickens and oil separates (6–8 minutes).

steps.text: Add the coriander leaves and lemon juice, check the salt and serve hot.

recipes.description: Tamil-style Aloo kari with sambar powder and curry leaves.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Wash, peel if needed and cut the potato into even, bite-sized pieces so they cook evenly.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, curry leaves and hing; add sambar powder for a Tamil kari flavour.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the potato and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on low flame for 12 minutes, stirring every few minutes. Sprinkle a little water only if it starts to stick.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with phulka, paratha or dal-rice.

tips: Cut vegetables to the same size so they cook evenly.
Cook on low heat with the lid on; the vegetables steam in their own moisture and need very little oil.
serving_ideas: phulka, paratha or bhakri, with dal and curd.
Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.

steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai, crackle the cumin, then add hing, green chilli and ginger and sauté for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the french beans and pumpkin and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on low flame for 12 minutes, stirring every few minutes. Sprinkle a little water only if it starts to stick.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with phulka, paratha or dal-rice.

tips: Cut vegetables to the same size so they cook evenly.
Cook on low heat with the lid on; the vegetables steam in their own moisture and need very little oil.
serving_ideas: phulka, paratha or bhakri, with dal and curd.
Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.

steps.text: Heat oil, crackle the cumin, add the onion and sauté until light golden. Add ginger, garlic and green chilli and cook for 1 minute.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the sweet corn kernels and tofu and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook uncovered
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 8 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until tender and lightly browned. Do not cover.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with phulka, paratha or dal-rice.

tips: Cut vegetables to the same size so they cook evenly.
Cook on low heat with the lid on; the vegetables steam in their own moisture and need very little oil.
serving_ideas: phulka, paratha or bhakri, with dal and curd.
Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.

steps.text: Wash, peel if needed and cut the cauliflower and lauki into even, bite-sized pieces so they cook evenly.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil in a kadhai, crackle the cumin, then add hing, green chilli and ginger and sauté for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the cauliflower and lauki and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on low flame for 12 minutes, stirring every few minutes. Sprinkle a little water only if it starts to stick.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with phulka, paratha or dal-rice.

tips: Cut vegetables to the same size so they cook evenly.
Cook on low heat with the lid on; the vegetables steam in their own moisture and need very little oil.
serving_ideas: phulka, paratha or bhakri, with dal and curd.
Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.

recipes.description: Karela tossed with crushed kadai spices, onion and capsicum.

steps.title: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Wash, peel if needed and cut the karela into even, bite-sized pieces so they cook evenly.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Dry-roast and crush the coriander seeds and red chillies. Heat oil, add cumin and the crushed spices, then the onion petals and capsicum, and toss for 2 minutes.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the karela and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook uncovered
steps.text: Cook on medium flame for 15 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until tender and lightly browned. Do not cover.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.

steps.text: Wash, peel if needed and cut the cabbage into even, bite-sized pieces so they cook evenly.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, add urad dal, curry leaves and hing; add sambar powder for a Tamil kari flavour.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Lower the flame and add the turmeric and powdered spices with 1 tbsp water so they do not burn. Stir for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the cabbage and salt and toss well to coat with the masala.

steps.title: Cook covered
steps.text: Cover and cook on low flame for 8 minutes, stirring every few minutes. Sprinkle a little water only if it starts to stick.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Uncover, raise the flame for 1 minute to dry any moisture, then add the coriander leaves and mix gently.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with phulka, paratha or dal-rice.

tips: Cut vegetables to the same size so they cook evenly.
Cook on low heat with the lid on; the vegetables steam in their own moisture and need very little oil.
serving_ideas: phulka, paratha or bhakri, with dal and curd.
Best time: lunch or dinner; also great in tiffin boxes.
recipes.storage: keeps in the fridge for 1–2 days.
